Central Nervous System
Physiology
Vision

Quick Overview

This lesson covers the functional structure of the retina, including the optic disc and the fovea, and the rod (scotopic) and cone (photopic) systems. It explains how photoreceptors generate a hyperpolarizing receptor potential, how the retina adapts to light and dark, and how colour is perceived. It then moves on to the visual field and binocular vision, and ends with the visual pathway from retina to cortex and the functions of areas 17, 18 and 19.

Functional Structure of the Retina

  • The retina contains the photoreceptors (rods and cones), which transform light into action potentials, plus the neural elements of the first and second order neurons of the visual pathway.
  • It is the only place where the body's arterioles can be seen directly (fundus examination).
  • It forms the innermost coat of the eyeball, extending as a thin membrane from the ora serrata (anteriorly) to the optic disc (posteriorly). It is separated from the vitreous humor by Müller's fibers.

Optic disc

  • Site of exit of the optic nerve; about 1.5 mm in diameter and about 3 mm to the nasal side. The central retinal artery enters, and the retinal vein exits, here.
  • It contains no photoreceptors, so it causes the physiological blind spot, demonstrated by the cross and circle experiment.
  • The blind spot is not noticed because of: (1) great overlap of the visual fields of both eyes; (2) the two blind spots do not lie at corresponding retinal points; (3) continuous fine movements of the eyeball.

Macula lutea and fovea centralis

  • Macula lutea: yellowish spot of about 1 mm², about 3 mm to the temporal side of the optic disc, opposite the posterior pole of the eye.
  • Fovea centralis: a pit-like depression of about 0.4 mm² in the centre of the macula. It is the area of greatest visual acuity because:
    • it contains only densely packed thin cones, with the other neural elements shifted to its surroundings, so light falls directly on the cones;
    • each cone connects to one bipolar cell, which connects to one ganglion cell with its own optic nerve fibre; this absence of convergence gives high acuity;
    • its pigmented epithelium is highly developed and markedly suppresses light reflection.
  • It is the only site in the body where point-to-point discrimination is exactly represented.
  • Photoreceptors are nourished from the choroid, whereas the neural elements (bipolar and ganglion cells) are nourished by the retinal vessels.

Fundus examination is done with an ophthalmoscope. Examining the retinal vessels helps diagnose atherosclerosis, diabetes, hypertension and many brain disorders.

Duplicity Theory of Vision

Because the retina has two types of receptors, there are two types of vision.

FeaturePhotopic vision (cones)Scotopic vision (rods)
Also calledDay or bright light visionDim or dark vision
NumberAbout 6 millionAbout 120 million
DistributionConcentrated centrally; the fovea contains cones onlyMainly peripheral; absent from the fovea
Light sensitivityLess sensitiveMuch more sensitive (higher photopigment concentration absorbs more light)
PhotopigmentAt least three typesOnly one: rhodopsin
ConnectionsIn the fovea, one cone to one bipolar to one ganglion cellAbout 200 rods converge on one bipolar cell; many bipolar cells converge on one ganglion cell
Detail and colourDetails, boundaries and colour well detectedDetails, boundaries and colour poorly detected; cannot distinguish colours
  • Some authors object to this theory: some animals have only cones but see in the dark, and others have only rods but see colours.
  • Purkinje phenomenon: in good daylight (photopic) yellow appears brightest, with the lowest threshold for stimulating the retina. In scotopic vision the maximal sensitivity shifts to blue-green.

Photoreceptor Stimulation and Receptor Potential

Photopigments

  • Rhodopsin (visual purple) in rod outer segments = protein scotopsin + 11-cis retinal (an aldehyde of vitamin A), the light-absorbing, curved part.
  • Cones contain photopsin (protein part: iodopsin) + retinal. There are three types, each sensitive to one primary colour: red, blue or green.
  • On exposure to light, rhodopsin decomposes very rapidly through metarhodopsin II to all-trans retinal (activated rhodopsin), a straight molecule separated from opsin.

Mechanism

In the darkIn the light
  • Na+ is pumped out of the inner segment and flows back in through outer-segment Na+ channels held open by cGMP (the dark Na+ current).
  • Resting membrane potential is low, only about -40 mV.
  • An inhibitory transmitter is released continuously, inhibiting synaptic transmission.
  • Activated rhodopsin activates cGMP phosphodiesterase, converting cGMP to 5'GMP and lowering cGMP.
  • Na+ channels close, causing hyperpolarization up to -70 mV.
  • Less inhibitory transmitter is released, which facilitates synaptic transmission along the visual pathway.

Photoreceptors are the only receptors in the body whose receptor potential is generated by hyperpolarization instead of depolarization. The receptor potential lasts longer in rods than in cones.

  • On removal of light: retinal isomerase inactivates all-trans retinal, cGMP is resynthesized, Na+ channels reopen and the potential returns to -40 mV, so the inhibitory transmitter is released again. This is most probably glutamate from cones (inhibits bipolar cells) and GABA from horizontal cells (inhibits on-center bipolar cells).

Changes in the retina on exposure to light

  • Structural: melanin spreads inside the pigmented cell layer to absorb the most light, preventing reflection and excessive stimulation.
  • Chemical: bleaching and degradation of the visual pigment.
  • Electrical: recorded as the electroretinogram (ERG), using one electrode on the cornea and one on the sclera. At rest there is a 6 mV potential difference, with the cornea positive.
ERG waveNatureAttributed to
aSmall negativeRods and cones
bBig positiveGanglion cells
cSlowly rising positive; can persist after light stopsPigmented cell layer
dSmall positiveLight cut-off

The ERG helps diagnose diseases when the retina cannot be seen because ocular fluids are cloudy. In retinitis pigmentosa (a degenerative retinal disease) the "a" wave is absent.

Retinal Adaptation

Adaptation is the ability of the retina to adjust its sensitivity to different light intensities. Sensitivity in maximal darkness is about 500,000 times that in maximal light adaptation.

Dark adaptation

  • Occurs when moving suddenly from strong light to a dark room; sensitivity to light markedly increases. Full adaptation takes about 30 minutes.
  • Pupillary dilatation (up to 8 mm) lets more light in.
  • Increased retinal sensitivity from regeneration of photopigments. Iodopsin in cones regenerates within 5 minutes (minor role); rhodopsin regenerates within 30 minutes, so rods play the major role.
  • Colours and details are less clear (visual acuity diminished).

Light adaptation

  • Occurs when passing suddenly from dark to bright light: light seems intense and annoying, with reflex lid closure, but normal sensation returns within about 5 minutes.
  • Pupillary constriction limits the light entering.
  • Breakdown of photopigments in rods and cones markedly reduces sensitivity.
  • Colours, details and boundaries are clearly seen (increased acuity).

Colour Vision

  • Colour vision is the discrimination of the wavelengths of the visible spectrum (red, orange, yellow, green, blue-green, blue, violet). Violet has the shortest wavelength (4000 Å) and red the longest (7000 Å).
  • Trained individuals can discriminate up to 200 colours. Colour vision is mainly a cone function and is highly developed in the fovea.

Definitions

  • Hue: the actual nature of the colour, depending on its wavelength.
  • Saturation: degree of purity of the colour from white.
  • Brightness (luminosity): intensity of the rays reflected from the colour, measured by photons emitted per unit area.
  • Primary colours: red, blue and green. Equal mixing of their wavelengths gives white, and mixing them can form any other spectral colour; they cannot be formed from other colours.
  • Complementary colours: each colour has one whose wavelengths, mixed in proper proportion, give white (e.g. yellow and deep blue, or red and greenish blue). This refers to mixing wavelengths, not pigments or paints.
  • Black: sensation produced by complete absence of light. A blind person sees "nothing" rather than black.
  • Retinas devoid of cones perceive shades of grey, so grey may be considered a rod-mediated form of colour vision.

Theories of colour vision

  • Trichromatic (Young-Helmholtz) theory: three cone types, maximally sensitive to blue-violet, green and red. Any coloured object stimulates all three unequally, giving a specific pattern of impulses; equal stimulation of all three gives white.
  • Neural theory: colour perception is mainly a function of a chain of neural cells, starting at X ganglion cells (stimulated by a colour in the central receptive field, inhibited by it in the peripheral field), then parvocellular neurons of the lateral geniculate body, then colour-sensitive "blob" neurons in the visual cortex, relaying to the lingual and fusiform gyri of the occipital cortex.
Ganglion cellProportionFunctionTermination
W cells40%Small; transmit rod visionDiffusely in the lateral geniculate body
X cells (P cells)55%Medium; transmit cone vision (acute and colour vision)Parvocellular part of the lateral geniculate body
Y cells (M cells)5%Large; respond to rapid changes in the image (movement or light intensity)Magnocellular part of the lateral geniculate body

Ganglion cells discharge continuously (5 to 40 per second) even when unstimulated in the dark.

Tests of colour vision

  • Colour matching test: separating coloured tufted wool into similar colours.
  • Ishihara's chart: figures printed in coloured circles on a coloured background; a normal person reads "5" where the patient reads "2", for example.
  • Edridge-Green lantern test: identifying the colour of a small illuminated area of variable size.

After-image phenomena

Normal visual sensations that persist after removal of the stimulus.

  • Positive after-image: after looking at a bright object briefly and closing the eyes, the image persists for seconds, due to reverberating circuits (after-discharge) in the retina or visual cortex.
  • Negative after-image: after looking at a bright coloured picture for at least 30 seconds then looking at a white surface, black parts appear white and white parts black (attributed to dark and light retinal adaptation), and coloured parts appear in their complementary colours. After-images move with the eye and enlarge when projected on a farther wall.

Visual Field

  • The visual field is the part of the external world seen by one eye fixed on a point. It is not circular: it is limited medially by the nose, superiorly by the orbital roof and inferiorly by the cheeks. Measuring it is called perimetry (using a perimeter).
  • For one eye it extends 80° downward, 50° upward, 60° nasally and more than 90° temporally.
  • Image position: temporal field objects focus on the nasal half of the retina, and nasal field objects on the temporal half. Objects in the lower left quadrant focus on the upper right quadrant of the retina.

Importance

  • Helps localize lesions in the visual pathway.
  • A blind area in the field is a scotoma, which may be due to optic nerve atrophy, retinal artery thrombosis, glaucoma, cataract or other pathway lesions. The optic disc causes the physiological blind spot.
  • Helps diagnose retinal diseases, e.g. retinitis pigmentosa, where blindness starts peripherally then involves the central field.

Binocular Vision

Binocular vision is the ability to use both eyes without diplopia (double vision). In humans and primates the eyes face forward, giving a large area of overlap of the two visual fields.

Requirements

  1. Large overlap of the visual fields, so the object forms an image on both retinas.
  2. Fusion of the two images into one, a function of the cerebral cortex; images must fall on corresponding retinal points.
  3. Accurate coordination of the external ocular muscles of both eyes; unequal action causes diplopia.
  4. Nearly equal dioptric power of both eyes; marked variation may cause diplopia.
  5. Intact visual cortex in the occipital lobe, the site of fusion.

Advantages

  • Masks optical defects of one eye by the overlapping field of the normal eye (not corrected if the defect is bilateral or involves corresponding retinal points; the two blind spots are not at corresponding points, so they are not seen).
  • The binocular field is larger than the monocular field, but less than the sum of both.
  • Depth perception (stereoscopic vision): discriminating relative distance and seeing objects in three dimensions. It is possible monocularly but better binocularly.
  • Better discrimination of colours.

Visual Pathway

Retina to optic chiasma

  • Photoreceptors stimulate bipolar cells (1st order neuron), which stimulate ganglion cells (2nd order neuron), whose axons form the optic nerve.
  • There are 126 million receptors but only 1.2 million optic nerve fibres. In the fovea the ratio of cones to bipolar to ganglion cells is 1:1:1, while peripherally up to 150 photoreceptors converge on one ganglion cell; central vision therefore has higher acuity but less sensitivity. About one third of optic nerve fibres come from the maculae.
  • At the optic chiasma there is partial decussation: fibres from the nasal half of each retina cross. Macular fibres also partially cross. Each optic tract therefore carries the temporal half of its own retina and the nasal half of the opposite retina.

Optic tract terminations

SiteFunction
Pretectal nucleusPupillary reflex
Superior colliculusVisuospinal reflexes controlling posture and equilibrium
Lateral geniculate bodyVisual fibres
Reticular formationArousal state
Suprachiasmatic nucleiCircadian rhythm

Lateral geniculate body and visual cortex

  • The lateral geniculate body (thalamus) is laminated into six cellular layers: crossed optic fibres end in layers 1, 4 and 6; uncrossed temporal fibres in layers 2, 3 and 5. There is point-to-point representation of the fovea. Fusion of the two eye images does not occur here; adjacent layers represent corresponding retinal points, sorting impulses for fusion in the cortex.
  • Its cells are the 3rd order neurons. Their axons form the optic radiation, passing through the retrolenticular part of the internal capsule to area 17 (visuosensory area) on the medial occipital lobe, responsible for conscious appreciation of vision.

Area 17 (primary visual cortex)

  • Extends to the tip of the occipital lobe and a little onto the lateral surface. Each area 17 receives impulses from the opposite halves of the visual fields of both eyes (left area perceives objects on the right).
  • Point-to-point retinal representation continues: upper retina above the calcarine fissure, lower retina below it. Peripheral vision is represented more anteriorly; central vision occupies a much larger posterior area extending to the tip and lateral surface.
  • Destruction of area 17 causes blindness of the opposite half of the visual field of both eyes (homonymous hemianopia).

Visual association areas (18 and 19)

  • Area 18 (visuopsychic): occupies a large region of the medial and lateral occipital surfaces, connected by short fibres with area 17. Area 19 (occipital eye field) lies in front of 18, extending into the posterior parietal lobe, with short fibres to 18 and long association fibres to other centres.
AreaFunctions
17Perception of visual sensations; fusion of the two retinal images; localization of objects in space relative to each other; perception of colour
18Understanding the meaning of seen objects; understanding written words; determining relative positions of objects
19Shares area 18's functions; sends information to other cortical areas (e.g. frontal eye field, area 8, during accommodation); integrates vision with other sensations; motor functions: conjugate deviation of both eyes to the opposite side, fixation movements, physiological nystagmus

Key Points / Quick Review

Retina

  • Optic disc: no photoreceptors, so the physiological blind spot.
  • Fovea: cones only, 1:1:1 connection, highest acuity.
  • Macula is 3 mm temporal to the disc; the disc is 3 mm nasal.

Rods vs cones

  • Cones (about 6 million): photopic, colour, acuity.
  • Rods (about 120 million): scotopic, one pigment (rhodopsin), high sensitivity, low acuity.
  • Purkinje shift: yellow to blue-green in dim light.

Phototransduction

  • Dark: cGMP keeps Na+ channels open, about -40 mV, inhibitory transmitter released.
  • Light: cGMP phosphodiesterase, cGMP falls, channels close, up to -70 mV.
  • Only receptors that hyperpolarize in response to stimulus.

ERG and adaptation

  • a: rods and cones; b: ganglion cells; c: pigment layer; d: light cut-off.
  • Dark adaptation: about 30 min, rods dominate, pupil dilates.
  • Light adaptation: about 5 min, pupil constricts, pigments break down.

Colour vision

  • Primary colours: red, blue, green; complementary pairs give white.
  • Trichromatic theory (three cone types) and neural theory (X ganglion, parvocellular LGB, blobs).
  • Ganglion cells: W 40%, X 55%, Y 5%.

Fields and binocular vision

  • Fields: 80° down, 50° up, 60° nasal, more than 90° temporal.
  • Binocular vision needs corresponding retinal points and cortical fusion.
  • Advantages: depth perception, larger field, masking defects, better colour discrimination.

Pathway

  • Bipolar (1st), ganglion (2nd), lateral geniculate body (3rd), then area 17.
  • Nasal retinal fibres cross at the chiasma; each tract carries the opposite visual field.
  • Radiation passes through the retrolenticular internal capsule.
  • Area 17 lesion gives homonymous hemianopia.

Optic tract targets and cortex

  • Pretectal: pupillary reflex; superior colliculus: visuospinal reflexes; reticular formation: arousal; suprachiasmatic: circadian rhythm.
  • Area 18: meaning of objects and written words; area 19: integration and eye movements.
